body.text: The federal government is inching closer to making a deal to pass its domestic gas reservation scheme through parliament, with a carve-out for WA.

Coalition won't follow One Nation's plans to slash humanitarian intake further
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has been out and about this afternoon, visiting a housing development in the electorate of Wright.

He's reiterated the Coalition's plan to tie migration with housing supply. Sticking with the topic of migration, he's asked what he thinks about One Nation's plan to cut the humanitarian intake by 90 per cent.
It's probably no surprise he thinks the Coalition's plan is "better", saying they've "got the balance right".

"We're going to oversee the biggest cuts to migration numbers in our country's history to provide breathing space for housing in this country but to keep the skilled migration this country needs," he says.
If elected, the Coalition wants to slash Australia's temporary migration intake by about 650,000 over four years through cuts to graduate, refugee and bridging visas.
Asked if the opposition would consider matching One Nation's plan to cap the refugee intake at 2,000 places, Taylor responded: "No".
"Some of the greatest Australians came here as refugees. some of those who have built the most successful businesses an extraordinary group of people," he says.
Shoebridge confirms Greens are revisiting Ukraine military aid policy
Greens leader David Shoebridge has confirmed reports in the Nine newspapers that party members are considering moves to end their opposition to Australian military aid being sent to Ukraine.
Earlier this year, Shoebridge told the Nine newspapers his party didn't support sending military aid to Ukraine unless it was approved by the UN Security Council.
Speaking at a press conference in Parliament House, Shoebridge says the Greens are "rock solid" in providing the same solidarity to Ukraine.

"Greens members have a right to actually engage in policy, and Greens members are engaging in policy on issues like Ukraine, on our climate policy, on our economic policy. It's how our party operates. We don't have policy dictated by the parliamentary team," Shoebridge says.

"Our policy on Ukraine is 100 per cent rock solid to provide the same solidarity to the people of Ukraine with their illegal invasion from Russia, as we do to the people of of Palestine for the illegal occupation by Israel."
Greens welcome superannuation test changes for riskier investments
The Greens have have welcomed the treasurer's plan to let superannuation funds place riskier investments in housing and renewable energy.
Jim Chalmers has proposed allowing super funds to invest 5 per cent of their portfolio in longer term "emerging assets" such as housing projects.
As reported by Tom Crowley, the intention is to allow funds to choose investments which may have low or uncertain returns today but higher returns tomorrow.
Greens senator Barbara Pocock says superannuation funds could contribute in a "significant way" to housing and renewable energy.

"We know we have the funds in our country to put a roof over every Australians' head, and superannuation funds potentially have a role to do that," Pocock says."We need ethical investment, safe investment by our superannuation funds, but they can contribute in a significant way to the major crises that face our country."
"We know we have the funds in our country to put a roof over every Australians' head, and superannuation funds potentially have a role to do that," Pocock says.
"We need ethical investment, safe investment by our superannuation funds, but they can contribute in a significant way to the major crises that face our country."
Trade unions push for under 18's to be paid super
Australian workers could be more than $12,000 better off in retirement if they were paid super when they were under 18, a parliamentary inquiry heard last night.
The inquiry is examining a Greens proposal to pay super to all workers under the age of 18, scrapping current eligibility rules that require a minimum 30 hours of work a week.
Joseph Mitchell from the Australian Council of Trade Unions says paying super should be non-negotiable.

"I was listening to the evidence from COSBOA (the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia)... that it would cost businesses $400 million, which is a straight out acknowledgement of just how much superannuation is stolen from workers," he said.
"Paying workers their minimum legal entitlements is the cost of doing business. That's it."
The inquiry heard that young women, regional and rural workers, and first nations workers are more likely to be impacted by not being paid super in their youth.
Gemma Killen, Executive Director of the Working with Women Alliance says women under 18 have 42% less super than men their age, which compounds to huge differences at retirement.

"We know that women under the age of 18 are more likely to work than their male peers... but they're more likely to work part time, and they're particularly concentrated in occupations with higher rates of casualisation".
Key Event
Senate argy-bargy over defence estate sales
The Senate has spent a chunk of time this morning arguing about the government's planned sell-off of defence properties around the country.
It's safe to say that the government's recent move to scrap the sale of sites like Victoria Barracks Sydney hasn't totally taken the heat out of this issue.
Some, like Liberal senator Jess Collins, have argued the site should remain an active military base — not be transformed into a museum, or put to other public use.
"I'll tell you what you don't do, if we're in the most strategically challenging time since World War Two," she said.
"You don't move the army out of Victoria Barracks Sydney, into a corporate block on Pitt St in Sydney — that doesn't have the facilities for them to do their job."
The government has frequently argued that the maintenance costs of sites like Victoria Barracks, which is 166-years old, should not be borne by Defence and personnel would be better placed elsewhere.

The Coalition, Greens and crossbenchers like David Pocock teamed up to suspend standing orders, and pass a motion condemning the government for moving Defence personnel out of the barracks, and calling on it to reverse course.
But despite the strong words — it's not a motion that will have any practical effect.
Key Event
The home affairs minister has defended Labor's backdown on working holiday visas yesterday, saying the changes have provided "a bit more headspace".
The federal government has increased the number of backpackers eligible for a third year visa from 5,000 to 25,000.
Working holiday makers would also be required to complete 120 days of regional work, increase of 88 days, to qualify for a second year visa.
Tony Burke says the changes will deliver for regional businesses and community.

"It's been a way to deliver what business needs, deliver what the regions need, while still delivering on the national expectation that we will manage the program in a way that matches the numbers that are in the budget," Burke says.
Burke says One Nation family visa plan will impact hospital, aged care sectors
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says One Nation's plan to slash family visas will lead to worker shortages in Australia's hospital, aged care and construction sectors.
Pauline Hanson today announced her party would scrap the parent visa program, which currently allows 7,000 parents and grandparents to migrate to Australia each year.
The One Nation leader also unveiled plans to cut Australia's humanitarian intake by 90 per cent to 2,000 places.
Speaking at a press conference in Newcastle, the home affairs minister says about half of the people who arrive in Australia on skilled visas wouldn't come if they couldn't bring family.
"Think about the hospital system. Half of the doctors on visas would not come. Half of the construction workers on visas would not come. It's even worse for aged care workers and nurses," Burke says.
"We can't run our hospital system without visas. We can't run our aged care system without visas."What One Nation is proposing is a complete attack on the services that Australians rely on."
"We can't run our hospital system without visas. We can't run our aged care system without visas.
"What One Nation is proposing is a complete attack on the services that Australians rely on."
Key Event
Albanese travels to China
Anthony Albanese is now on his way to China for the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
They don't call it 'summit season' for no reason — this is the prime minister's third country in just over a week.

But Albanese is likely to be a bit of a footnote at this year's APEC with all eyes on a looming trilateral meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin due Thursday.
Still, the Australian PM has a busy schedule — including his own meeting with Xi come Friday.
On his first day in Shenzhen, Albanese will be making a stop to mark Australia's strong trade ties with China and also attending a CEO roundtable.
Defence officials learned of Victoria Barracks backflip days before it was announced

Senior Defence officials guiding the department's sale of more than 60 sites around the country have revealed they were told about recent backflips on a number of key sites just days before the announcement was made.

Earlier this month Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the government would scrap plans to sell four defence sites — Victoria Barracks Sydney, Victoria Barracks Melbourne, Point Cook and Fort Queenscliff.
The sale of Victoria Barracks Sydney had attracted significant protest, with figures from Greens leader David Shoebridge to former prime minister John Howard opposing the move.
At a parliamentary hearing last night, defence officials were asked when they were told of the change in plans.
"The nature of the substance of the announcement, I was consulted on in the days prior to (the announcement)," said Deputy Secretary Security and Estate, Celia Perkins.
She told the hearing it was a decision of "government, of ministers".
ADF personnel and Defence staff will move out of Victoria Barracks Sydney in coming weeks, before the site is handed to the Department of Finance early next year.
While the sites will remain in public hands, it's still somewhat unclear who will manage the site into the future.
Government, not Iran war, driving cost of living pressures: Hanson
Australia's cost of living crisis is not a result of the war in Iran, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says.
Hanson was asked whether it was time for US President Donald Trump to end the conflict, given the global oil shock is one of the drivers of high inflation.
The One Nation leader says that's up to Trump to decide and that Iran shouldn't have nuclear weapons.
On the cost of living, she pointed to the government's "bad management" for driving up inflation.
"It's out of control, spending by the current government, by the treasurer, and the waste of money that's happening in this place is unbelievable," Hanson says.
She says that's a point Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has been making too.
Bullock has said recent interest rate rises have been to deal with "domestic capacity pressures" but also that the Middle East war was a contributing factor.
Key Event
Hanson denies policy 'slams door shut' on certain refugees
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has denied her new migration policy was designed to "slam the door shut" on any particular group of refugees.
Under the plan the humanitarian intake would be slashed by 90 per cent, down from 20,000 places to 2,000.
Hanson is asked if she was closing the door to people fleeing moderate Muslims and Christians facing persecution in countries like Iran, Pakistan and Indonesia.
She disagrees with that suggestion.
"I'm not slamming the door shut at all. We're saying 2000 people, that's the limit," Hanson says.
Hanson quizzed on plans for 150,000 parents already waiting for visa
Around 150,000 parents of migrants are already in the queue for a parent visa. Some of them are in Australia already on bridging visas.
One Nation's Pauline Hanson is asked what happens to those people? Are they deported?
Hanson says that if One Nation is elected to government, those waiting will get a refund on their applications and if they're in Australia they'll have to leave.
She said if they wanted to stay then they would need to apply for a temporary sponsored parent visa.
"They can get a visa for ... even up to 10 years. But the families will have to pay for it," she says.
Hanson defended the scrapping of the parent visa program by saying Australia couldn't afford to provide aged care and hospital beds for existing residents.
Hanson confirms One Nation plan to slash refugee intake by 90 per cent
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has just stepped up for a press conference.
She's confirming the second phase of the party's migration plan: slashing the humanitarian intake by 90 per cent, to 2,000 places. It currently sits around 20,000 places.
The parent visa program would also be scrapped. The family migration scheme currently allows about 7,000 parents and grandparents to migrate to Australia each year.
Hanson says Australia "can't afford" the scheme any longer.
WA carve-out from gas reservation scheme a 'good start': Hume
Liberal deputy Jane Hume has described WA's carve-out from the proposed gas reservation scheme as a "good first start".

The Coalition had been pushing for a carve-out in negotiations for its support for the scheme, which would force Australia's largest gas exporters to retain up to 20 per cent of their product for the domestic market.

A last-minute deal between WA and the federal government was struck this morning. It would set the state's gas obligation under the scheme to zero as it already has its own state-based system in place.
Asked if the deal was enough to get the Coalition's support, Hume says there are other sticking points that need to be addressed.
"We still need to make sure that any reservation scheme that is established doesn't turn away new investment," she tells News 24.

"There are ways to fix this. We do want to help the government get to a solution where we can have a gas reservation for domestic use, but we also don't want to discourage new investment and export opportunities."
Chalmers announces plan to let super funds place riskier investments

Super funds will be able to take riskier, longer-term bets with their members' money, in an overhaul of fund rules which Treasurer Jim Chalmers hopes will promote investment in housing, energy and startups.

Under changes to the performance test, a benchmarking exercise introduced by former treasurer Josh Frydenberg, Chalmers will propose to let super funds invest 5 per cent in so-called "emerging assets" with a lower minimum return.

The intention is to allow funds to choose investments which may have low or uncertain returns today but higher returns tomorrow, such as early-stage housing developments or renewable projects or venture capital funds.
Funds will not be required to invest in housing, energy or any sector, or to use the new option at all, and their obligation to invest in members' best interest would not change.

But the move hands a win to some industry super funds who have argued the current benchmarks, measured relative to average stock market returns year by year, have prevented them from making long-term investments with irregular return patterns

Minerals Council rubbishes budget office's mining tax take

The mining industry group has panned the Parliamentary Budget Office's analysis of the former Rudd government's abandoned mining tax, which the independent agency said could have raised $135 billion if it was kept.

The Greens commissioned the PBO to look at how much the tax on mining super profits pitched by former prime minister Kevin Rudd could have raised if it was not watered down and then ultimately scrapped by the Coalition.
The PBO said in its conclusion that $135 billion would have been raised since 2012, it had assumed no change in production or investment behaviour by the big mining companies.
Minerals Council of Australia chief executive Tania Constable says that puts the analysis in the realm of "pure conjecture"

"Its assumption that a giant new mining tax would have no impact on mining company behaviour is clearly nonsensical," Constable says."In their rush to demonise and vilify the mining sector as part of their class warfare crusade, the Greens have once again exposed themselves as economically illiterate."
"Its assumption that a giant new mining tax would have no impact on mining company behaviour is clearly nonsensical," Constable says.
"In their rush to demonise and vilify the mining sector as part of their class warfare crusade, the Greens have once again exposed themselves as economically illiterate."
Key Event
Cook confirms deal done on WA carve-out for gas reservation scheme
WA Premier Roger Cook has confirmed he's reached an agreement with the federal government on a change to the proposed gas reservation scheme.
The premier had issued a call for WA senators to "stand up" as the bill was debated in parliament this week.
Under the initial proposal, gas exporters would be required to retain up to 20 per cent of their product for the domestic market.
Essentially, his argument was that, because WA has its own state-based scheme to force exporters to reserve supply for the domestic market, it shouldn't have been included in the national scheme.

That argument was knocked back by the government, who argued it was a matter of constitutionality that WA had to be included. Resources Minister Madeleine King said she'd use ministerial discretion to set WA's obligation to zero.
But Cook says an agreement has been reached to make that permanent and called on the parliament to "get behind" the amendment.
"The Albanese government listened to WA by separating the west coast from the east coast gas market in their draft legislation," he says in a statement.
"They then created the ability for the federal minister to set WA's domestic gas supply obligation to zero under their scheme — recognising our own system is already delivering 20 per cent.
"They have now proposed an amendment that would make a zero domestic supply obligation setting permanent."Together, these settings will create an effective carve out for WA."
"They have now proposed an amendment that would make a zero domestic supply obligation setting permanent.
"Together, these settings will create an effective carve out for WA."

WA's inclusion in the scheme has been a real sticking point for the opposition. We're expecting Angus Taylor to stand up later this morning, so we'll soon find out whether this deal does enough to secure the Coalition's support.
Sweeping changes proposed to nation’s surrogacy laws
The country's law reform body has recommended surrogates be entitled to greater financial compensation for the impacts of pregnancy and childbirth.

The wide-ranging final report from the Australian Law Reform Commission, tabled in parliament overnight, found Australia's patchwork of state and territory laws made surrogacy unnecessarily difficult.

As part of its 47 recommendations, it said there should be one nationally consistent surrogacy framework overseen by a regulator and proposed intended parents be recognised as legal parents from birth.
While it said a ban on commercial surrogacy should be maintained, it recommended an expansion of what surrogates could be compensated for, so they weren't left financially disadvantaged.
The federal government says it'll consider the recommendations alongside the states and territories.
You can read more about the report at the link below.
Greens edging closer on CGT and trusts, but no deal done yet: McKim
Greens Treasury spokesperson Nick McKim also took a turn in the ABC Radio National Breakfast hot seat this morning.
The minor party is the only pathway the government has for passing two major tax bills: the changes to the capital gains tax (CGT) discount and a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts.
"I'd describe the negotiations as constructive, but we don't yet have an agreement to pass either of those pieces of legislation this year," he says.
McKim says he's hopeful of landing a resolution on CGT. Pushed if the Greens were getting closer to a deal, he responded: "I think you could probably couch it like that."
On trusts, as my colleague Tom Crowley reported yesterday, the main sticking point is a concern that an exemption for charitable giving is too broad.
"We don't see why they should get a tax benefit for donations like that when someone like you, or I, doesn't get that benefit as ordinary wage earners," he says.
Key Event
Ending parent visas 'very harsh', Wong says
Foreign Minister Penny Wong says One Nation's plan to axe parent visas for migrants would be "very harsh" and has rejected the party's claims that Australia's refugee intake is too high.

Nine Newspapers are reporting One Nation's proposal includes a wholesale scrapping of the family migration scheme which currently allows about 7,000 parents and grandparents to migrate to Australia each year.
Leader Pauline Hanson also wants to reduce the refugee intake from 20,000 to just 2,000.
Wong says Australia makes a "very small contribution" in its refugee intake and accuses One Nation of seeking to "divide" Australians.

"When I deal with other countries, one of the things I talk about is who we are in Australia," she says."Australia is an extraordinary country and country, which is informed by, the richness of First Nations cultures, and everyone who has arrived since."
"When I deal with other countries, one of the things I talk about is who we are in Australia," she says.
"Australia is an extraordinary country and country, which is informed by, the richness of First Nations cultures, and everyone who has arrived since."
One Nation has argued that its proposed intake of 2,000 refugees is above the OECD average, which Wong rejects.
"There are countries which take more refugees, there are countries which countries which take fewer. We think this is the right balance," she says.
WA carve-out just one of four issues Coalition has with gas reservation scheme
A proposal to require Australia's biggest gas exporters to set aside 20 per cent of their product for the domestic market is currently being debated in the Senate.

The government needs support from either the Coalition or the Greens to get the gas reservation scheme over the line. But West Australia's inclusion, which already has a state-based scheme, has been a sticking point for the opposition.
Shadow Resources Minister Susan McDonald is asked if WA was able to negotiate an amendment and whether the Coalition would agree to support it.
McDonald tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast that's just one of four issues the opposition has.

"Certainly the Western Australian carve-out is an important point, and it is one of the four. But we also have problems with the must-sell provisions without reciprocal responsibilities on the buyer," she says.

"We have problems with the 110 per cent oversupply. We have massive concerns that we have that we are constructing legislation that completely relies on ministerial interventions rather than something that is transparent and well regulated and clear."
Backpacker visa changes sent wrong message to young workers: McDonald
Nationals frontbencher Susan McDonald has taken aim at the government's migration plan, declaring it sends the wrong message to backpackers.

The government yesterday backed down on planned changes to working holiday visas, increasing the number of places available for third-year visas while also increasing how much time young people need to work in the bush to stay in Australia.
But McDonald argues Labor had already done "incredible damage" to businesses who rely on seasonal workers.

"They have sent such a strong message to backpackers that they're not welcome ... They've done incredible damage right at the beginning of the Christmas season for tourism businesses and of course for the motels, hotels, truck stops and other businesses that reply on these seasonal workers," she told ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
On British backpackers, who under a Morrison-era free trade deal aren't required to do regional work, McDonald says she'd love to see "more young Brits get out to regional places".
"I'd love to see that the young Brits get out of Sydney and Melbourne and get out to the regions. They'll have a great time."
Key Event
One Nation unveils plan for massive cut to refugee intake
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says her party will target humanitarian visas to bring down net migration levels.
The Nine Newspapers are reporting the plan would include slashing the refugee intake by 90 per cent and barring migrants from bringing their parents to Australia.
Hanson stopped to talk to reporters as she entered Parliament House this morning and said while Australia was "built on migration", it "can't afford it any longer".
"What we're looking at is humanitarian and those people coming here to stay in Australia," she says.
Asked about Australia's legal and moral commitments in its refugee resettlement program, Hanson says Australia is "still above the OECD numbers in the world".
It's not clear exactly what numbers she's referring to, but it could be Australia's per capita refugee intake compared to other OECD economies.
A recent OECD report shows Australia was among the top three resettling countries as of 2022, behind the (11,539), Canada (10,500).
Reducing the refugee intake to 2,000 places would place Australia well down that list.
Bowen backs COP31 electrification push
Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen says the world needs to rapidly increase electrification to 35 per cent of global energy consumption to slow the rate of global warming.
"Moving to more electricity and less direct fossil fuel use is absolutely vital," Bowen told ABC's 7.30 from COP31 in Turkiye.
"The world has been creeping up at about 0.3 per cent. We need to really increase that progress by fourfold to keep the world at 1.5 degrees of warming.

"Electrification has really been the unfinished frontier. We're dealing with renewable energy, but things that are directly done by fossil fuels, whether it is gas in industry, or home cooking in Africa — you know, there's a wide gambit of uses of fossil fuels that really can be done better by electricity.
"Same as transport. If you move from an internal combustion engine to an electric car — even if the grid is fossil fuels based, you're massively reducing emissions."
Key Event
What does Wong want to see from Trump's meetings with Xi and Putin?
US President Donald Trump is expected to meet with China's Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong called the meeting of the two world leaders important and encouraged them to engage in dialogue.

"We know that they are in competition economically. We know that they are in competition strategically, and what Australia wants, what the region wants, what the world wants, is for there to be, you know ... make sure that there is a dialogue," she tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.

"A capacity for continued peace and stability that requires the great powers to talk to one another."So we always encourage the US and China to engage and ensure that the competition that we live with does not escalate into something we do not wish to see."
"A capacity for continued peace and stability that requires the great powers to talk to one another.
"So we always encourage the US and China to engage and ensure that the competition that we live with does not escalate into something we do not wish to see."
Trump will also meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the summit. Wong says she hopes the US president would put pressure on Putin to end the war in Ukraine.
"This is a war that is unjust. This is a war that is in breach of the UN Charter. This is a war that is weighing on civilians in Ukraine. And it is a war that should end," she says.
Albanese comes face to face with Trump at Quad meeting
US President Donald Trump has prompted new defence, critical minerals and technology initiatives alongside Anthony Albanese and the leaders of India and Japan at the first Quad summit in two years.
The meeting in Manila comes ahead of Trump's visit to China, with the four-nation grouping widely seen as a counterweight to Beijing's influence in the Indo-Pacific.
Trump says the countries have struck new critical minerals deals to protect supply chains from economic coercion and will conduct a joint exercise involving maritime patrol aircraft.
"We have a lot of things happening over the next 12 months that will very much surprise people," he said overnight.
The US president also talks up his personal relationships with the other leaders.
"We're all friends. It's a lot easier that way," he said.
Albanese has said the four countries working together represent "greater than the sum of just the individual parts".
Key Event
Quad leaders meeting a 'signal' nations will continue to cooperate
Foreign Minister Penny Wong also popped up on ABC's News Breakfast this morning, where she was asked about the Quad leaders meeting overnight.
It's the first time the leaders from Australia, the US, Japan and India have met int wo years.
But Wong points out the grouping's foreign ministers have actually met three times this year alone.

"I'm really pleased that we're seeing at that summit a meeting at leader level. I think it's a signal that these four countries will continue to cooperate, will continue to provide benefits whether it's maritime surveillance or building cables," she says.

"We've together made sure that every Pacific island country is now connected with cable connectivity. So there are practical benefits to that cooperation. It's very important for stability in the region."
Australia to keep advocating with China on iron ore: Wong
Anthony Albanese will today depart Manila for the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong is asked whether Albanese would raise the issue of China's centra purchasing agency for iron ore deals. The Australian Financial Review suggested earlier this week Australia could lose as much as $10b over the next decade as a result.
Wong tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast that negotiations are currently taking place.
"We always advocate for open and fair trade. We do that generally and we've done that specifically with China," she says.

"You've seen, as a consequence of that advocacy and our engagement with China, we've seen trade impediments worth billions of dollars to the Australian economy lifted over the last few years."We'll continue to take that same approach when it comes to iron ore," she says.
"You've seen, as a consequence of that advocacy and our engagement with China, we've seen trade impediments worth billions of dollars to the Australian economy lifted over the last few years.
"We'll continue to take that same approach when it comes to iron ore," she says.
Wong spoke to Israeli counterpart last night
Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirms she spoke with her Israeli counterpart about Australia's latest round of sanctions.

"I outlined our position ... I said we do not agree with, we oppose the settlement activities. We have had a long-standing position on this. We've made it clear we will continue to take action in respect to those involvement in the settlement enterprise," she says.
She's also asked if Australia is concerned about Israel's response to the sanctions.
Wong says Israel has already taken action Australia for other sanctions, such as when targeted financial sanctions and travel bans were applied to ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotric.
"We've seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah.

"We've also seen the caretaker Prime Minister Netanyahu be very public in his criticism of Australia."So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do."
"We've also seen the caretaker Prime Minister Netanyahu be very public in his criticism of Australia.
"So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do."
Key Event
Increase in settler attacks last month behind Australia's fresh sanctions
Foreign Minister Penny Wong says fresh sanctions on Israeli settlers are in response to a spike in settler violence in the West Bank last month.
Three individuals, including Daniella Weiss and the settlement advocacy group she founded and leads, have been sanctioned by the Australian government.
Weiss was sanctioned by the UK last year, and EU earlier this year. Wong tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast that Australia has been coordinating with the UK on sanctions.
But she says we've moved today because of the increase in violence in October.

"We've seen an increase in settlement attacks in the month of October, recorded by the UN, and we also know the E1 settlement ... the final decisions are being made on that by the caretaker Israeli government on the 19th of November," Wong says.
The E1 development, east of Jerusalem, would effectively divide the West Bank in two.
"We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement."
Wong was asked if there was any intelligence Australia investment was going to Israeli settlements. She say she doesn't have detailed information about "what individuals might be doing or not doing".

"But what I can say is from the government's perspective, the action we can take is to sanctions individuals and entities so that it is against the law for people to provide that financial support," she says.
Timor-Leste PM shares joke with Albanese at ASEAN
Timor-Leste's Prime Minister Xanana Gusmão brought a bit of humour to his meeting with Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Manila overnight.
The veteran leader poked his head through the door as he arrived, jokingly asking: "Can I come in?"
Gusmão also made light of a viral photograph of himself smoking, gesturing as though he's holding a cigarette.
And when Albanese congratulated him on Timor-Leste's plans to host ASEAN in 2029, Gusmão jokingly covered his face with his hands.
There are some serious business on the agenda too, with the leaders discussing the long-running Greater Sunrise gas project.
Albanese reiterated his commitment to progressing its development in line with the 2018 maritime boundary treaty.
Key Event
Fresh sanctions for West Bank settlers
Australia has announced fresh sanctions targeting individuals and organisations over illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank.
Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong says three people and four organisations have been sanctioned, including for the first time a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The measures mean Australians people and businesses are banned from trading with or providing financial or other support to those sanctioned.
Penalties for breaching sanctions include up to 10 years' imprisonment.
Good morning 👋
Hello friends. Welcome to our politics live blog. I'm Courtney Gould from the ABC's Parliament House team, here to guide you through the day.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong will be out and about this morning discussing Australia's latest round of sanctions targeting individuals and organisations over illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank.
Overnight, Anthony Albanese met with the Quad leaders in Manila. It's the first time the talks between the leaders of Australia, the US, India and Japan have been held in two years.
There's a bit going on this morning, so let's dive right in.
